findings.title: Device tagging now runs synchronously on the anonymous auth hot path
findings.body: Previously TagDevice ran in a background goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout; this PR makes it a blocking call inside Anonymous.Authenticate using the request context. Every anonymous request now performs at least one (and when a device limit is configured, two: COUNT + INSERT/UPDATE) synchronous database round trips before the request is authenticated. This adds DB latency to every anonymous page load/API call and, if the DB is slow or the request context is cancelled mid-write, anonymous authentication itself fails. The device-limit enforcement could have stayed asynchronous, or only the limit-exceeded path made synchronous.

findings.title: Device limit check is a TOCTOU race (COUNT then INSERT, no transaction or unique constraint logic)
findings.body: CreateOrUpdateDevice first runs CountDevices and then, if count < limit, executes an upsert in a separate session. Under concurrent requests from distinct devices, many goroutines can observe count < limit simultaneously and all insert, exceeding the configured device limit by an arbitrary amount. There is no transaction, no locking, and no conditional insert. If the limit is meant to be a hard cap (e.g., for licensing), it can be materially exceeded under load.

findings.title: Changed constructor/provider signatures with no visible update to DI registration
findings.body: ProvideAnonDBStore gained a `deviceLimit int64` parameter and ProvideAnonymousDeviceService changed its third parameter from `anonstore.AnonStore` to `db.DB`. The PR contains no changes to the fx/wire registration (e.g., pkg/server) that supplies these providers. If the registration still lists `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` in a provider set, fx cannot satisfy the new `int64` argument and startup will fail; if it passed an AnonStore value to ProvideAnonymousDeviceService, the build breaks. The wiring change should be included in the PR (and the removed injection of an AnonStore also breaks any test doubles/Enterprise consumers of that provider signature).

findings.title: anonymousDeviceLimit always serialized (0 when unset), conflicting with frontend type `number | undefined`
findings.body: The DTO field is `int64` with no `omitempty`, so the frontend always receives `anonymousDeviceLimit: 0` even when no limit is configured. The TS type declares `number | undefined`, and GrafanaBootConfig defaults it to `undefined`, so consumers distinguishing 'no limit' from 'limit of 0' will see inconsistent values depending on whether backend or frontend defaults won the merge. Either use a pointer with omitempty, or make the frontend type `number` with a documented 0-means-unlimited semantic.

findings.title: updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for devices that exist but expired
findings.body: When the limit is reached, updateDevice only updates rows whose updated_at is within [UpdatedAt-30d, UpdatedAt+1min]. A returning device whose row is older than 30 days (but younger than the 61-day cleanup retention) matches zero rows, so the caller gets ErrDeviceLimitReached and the user is denied anonymous access — the same error as an entirely new device. More importantly, the error name is misleading for this case and, in client.go, any ErrDeviceLimitReached from Authenticate is surfaced as an auth failure to the user with no differentiation; consider whether an expired-device renewal should evict/replace rather than hard-fail.

findings.title: No test that an existing device is successfully updated when the limit is reached
findings.body: The new test only covers the rejection path (second distinct device fails with ErrDeviceLimitReached). There is no test asserting the intended behavior that a *known* device can still refresh (update) its row when count >= limit, nor a test with deviceLimit=0 confirming the limit is disabled. The updateDevice path (rowsAffected > 0) has no coverage at all.

findings.title: Query string passed as first Exec argument via args slice is fragile
findings.body: updateDevice (and the existing upsert) prepend the query into the args slice and call dbSession.Exec(args...). This works only if the session's Exec signature is (query, args...); passing the query through an `[]interface{}` is unusual and breaks if the Exec implementation type-checks or logs parameters, and it obscures intent. Additionally, `args` is captured and mutated inside the WithDbSession closure while also being the outer variable; a retry of the session callback (xorm retries transactions in some configurations) would re-prepend the query to an already-prepended slice on a second invocation, producing an invalid call.
